text:
In the Court of Appeal of Alberta

Citation: R. v. Keegstra, 1991 ABCA 97

Date:
19910313

Docket:
17699
& 17701

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

(Respondent re Conviction)

(Appellant re Sentence)

- and -

James Keegstra

Accused

(Appellant re Conviction)

(Respondent re Sentence)

The Court:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Kerans

The Honourable Mr. Justice Irving

Supplementary Reasons for Judgment of the Court

APPEAL FROM THE JUDGMENT OF THE HONOURABLE
MR. JUSTICE MacKENZIE OF THE COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH OF ALBERTA DATED THE 20TH
DAY OF JULY, 1987.

COUNSEL:

Bruce R. Fraser, Esq., Q.C. and L.K. Phillippe,
Esq., for the Respondent re Conviction Appellant re Sentence

D.H. Christie, Esq. and Duncan L. McKillop,
Esq., for the Appellant re Conviction Respondent re Sentence

SUPPLEMENTARY
REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE COURT

I.

[
1
]

These are Reasons for decision supplementary to
those earlier reported. See (1988)
1988 ABCA 234 (CanLII)
, 43 CCC (3d) 150.

[
2
]

One ground of appeal is that the learned trial
judge deprived the accused of the right of challenge of a juror for cause.

[
3
]

It is trite law that an accused has the right,
in appropriate circumstances, to challenge a prospective juror for cause: see
ss. 638-640 C.C.C. It is also clear that to deny this right to an accused
affects the fairness of the trial procedure in a significant way, and an error
of this sort cannot be protected by s. 686(1)(b)(iii). See
R. v. Leaney

(1979)
1989 CanLII 28 (SCC)
, 71 C.R. (3d) 325 (S.C.C.)

[
4
]

The
right
to challenge for cause must be
considered separately from the
procedure
on a challenge. The procedure
is to commence an inquiry into partiality, and this might take the form of
questions put to the prospective juror. We do not pass on the adequacy of the
proposed questions in this case. The substance of them was that the prospective
jurors be asked about awareness of pre-trial publicity and its effect on them.

[
5
]

The accused, then, proposed to challenge all
prospective jurors on the array for cause. It is clear also that the
application on behalf of the accused at the opening of jury selection, although
made very clumsily, was correctly understood by the learned trial judge as such
a challenge. He said (A.B. 130):

The accused applies for leave to
challenge prospective jurors for cause on the ground that they are [not]
indifferent, due to the very extensive pretrial publicity about the accused and
about the case, which it is alleged has given rise to a bias in the community
of such an extent that according to the argument of the accused it is necessary
to question witnesses before they are allowed to take the jurors' oath.

[
6
]

We have added the word "not" to this
quotation because the learned trial judge acknowledged within moments of the
statement that he had failed to do so by reason of a slip of the tongue.

[
7
]

The decision of the learned trial judge was that
no inquiry should be commenced. It is said for the accused that the learned
trial judge made a reviewable error. In our opinion, he did.

[
8
]

It is clear on the authorities that the right of
an accused to challenge a juror for cause is, while strong, not unqualified.
The Ontario Court of Appeal, in

Hubbert v. R.

1975 CanLII 53 (ON CA)
, 29 C.C.C. (2d) 279 at 289 (appeal dismissed by S.C.C.
1976 CanLII 1457 (SCC)
, 33
C.C.C. (2d) 207) said:

There is an initial presumption that a
juror not disqualified by the statute under which he is selected, will perform
his duties in accordance with his oath.

[
9
]

The Court added at page 291:

Trials should not be unnecessarily
prolonged by speculative and sometimes suspect challenges for cause.

[
10
]

The Court then referred to abuse of this
procedure in other jurisdictions, and said that trial judges in Canada had discretion to prevent abuse. We
affirm this view.

[
11
]

On the other hand,
Hubbert
is authority
for the proposition that the accused need not, as a condition precedent to a
challenge, establish that the prospective juror is in fact irretrievably
partial. The very purpose of the challenge for cause is to inquire into that
issue.

[
12
]

In our view, the learned trial judge correctly
charged himself when he said this:

From these cases, I extract the
principles, first, the jurors will be presumed to act on their oath to give a
true verdict, and, therefore, it should not be subjected unnecessarily to
inquisitions on a simple speculation or a mere chance that they may be -- or,
may not be indifferent. Secondly, that the modern juror will quite possibly
have some preconceived ideas. I would add, quite likely will have some
preconceived ideas because we live in a literate society. People read. They
read newspapers. They watch television. So it's likely that they will have
preconceived ideas about a particular accused's guilt or innocence. But given
the sophistication, education, and intelligence of most Canadians, they will
respond to the requirement of the law and directions of the Trial Judge, and
obey their oath, notwithstanding any previously formed opinions. Third, the
strength of the jury system is actually found in what many perceive to be its
weakness. Namely, its diversity and the individual imperfections and qualities
of each of its members. That is why we choose 12, rather than one or two jurors
to try the case.

(A.B. 133)

[
13
]

Our difficulty arises when he applied these
considerations to this case.

[
14
]

He rejected the application on the ground that
he was not satisfied that pre-trial publicity here would have persuaded:

… citizens who are burdened with an oath
and charged by law not to convict a person unless they're satisfied beyond a
reasonable doubt that a certain set of facts has been proven to exist, and
which they must apply to specific rules of law.

In short, the mere fact of very extensive
pre-trial publicity, at least in this particular case, I find is soggy ground
and provides too unsure a footing to support an argument that there is a
possibility of bias in the prospective jurors which should give rise to their
being subjected to examination before being allowed to take their Juror's Oath.
The argument is too implausible to support the finding that the necessary
foundation for a challenge for cause on the ground of a lack of indifference
has been established.

(A.B. 134-135)

[
15
]

In our view, the substance of the decision of
the learned trial judge was that to permit a challenge for cause in the
circumstances of this case would amount to an abuse of the right of challenge.
To use his own earlier words, he apparently was satisfied that the suggestion
of possible partiality from publicity in this case was "simple
speculation" and "mere chance".

[
16
]

We admire the confidence of the learned trial
judge in the effect of an oath upon the citizens of Canada. Moreover, we tend to agree. In most cases, the impact of pre-trial
publicity can be easily overcome by one or more of these procedures: the oath,
a specific warning by the trial judge, a delay of the trial, or a change of
venue. For example, the employment of one or more of these means should insure
that any
new
trial here will be fair. It is only in
very special
circumstances
that the pre-trial publicity alone would cause a judge to
permit a challenge for cause.

[
17
]

We agree with the learned trial judge that, even
at the first trial, it was
likely
that the accused would be given an
impartial trial by all the prospective jurors. Nevertheless, the question the
Court must ask itself is whether there was, on the material before the learned
trial judge, any reason to
doubt
that the impartiality of any one of the
prospective jurors might have been affected irretrievably. In our respectful
view, there was.

[
18
]

We should say in this regard that we have the
benefit of the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in
R. v. Zundel

1987 CanLII 121 (ON CA)
, 1987 31 C.C.C. (3d) 97; leave to S.C.C. dismissed
(1988) 61 O.R. (2d) 289
. The
pre-trial publicity in this case was not unlike that in
Zundel
.
The
learned trial judge in
Zundel
also denied a challenge for cause. The
Ontario Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. This decision, while published
well before argument before us in this case, was not available to the learned
trial judge.

[
19
]

The accused filed a large collection of press
clippings and the like at the time of the application. See Voir Dire Exhibit 3;
Notebooks of Newspaper clippings; entered A.B. 114. The learned trial judge did
not refer to the exhibit, but said:

… I take judicial notice of the fact that
throughout Alberta … the
accused has been the subject of wide media attention right up to the date of.
the trial … This has been a matter of continuing widespread public debate. Few,
if any, members of the public escaped the onslaught. Most members of the
public, if they're honest, must have some kind of tentative opinion about the
accused.

(A.B. 134)

[
20
]

In order to underline the uniqueness of the case,
however, we think it wise to emphasize some facts:

(1)
Duration.

[
21
]

The specifics of the charge against the
appellant were that he had, while exercising the status of a high school
teacher between 1978 and 1982, preached hatred of Jews to his students in the
guise of social studies lessons. The accused had been dismissed from his job in
1982, but did not go to trial until 1985. The publicity continued unceasingly
from the one event to the other.

(2)
Affirmation by the Courts.

[
22
]

A Queen's Bench Judge, sitting as a Board of
Reference under the
School Act
, R.S.A. 1980, c. S-3, heard an appeal of
the dismissal and found as a fact that the accused had made scandalous
statements in the classroom. See
Keegstra v. Board of Education
(1983)
45 A.R. 348
. This decision, published April 15, 1983, was given widespread and,
of course, legitimate publicity.

(3)
Questions about communal acceptance.

[
23
]

The allegation was that he had been permitted to
continue in this practice during many years while in the
public
employ.
This raised the troubling question whether the community in which he lived and
worked agreed with him. That question was further stirred by the fact that he
had been elected Mayor of the town where he lived. As a result, much of the
publicity about the case centred, over several years, more on the issue of
possible communal acceptance of his views than on
his
guilt or
innocence. In the eyes of the media, his fellow citizens were on trial along
with the accused.

[
24
]

Premier Lougheed had felt compelled to say this
in the Legislature, in 1983:

… I was deeply disturbed with the
confirmation that a certificated teacher in this province's schools had been
able to transmit, over an extended period of time, views that were clearly
racial and religiously prejudiced, and anti-Semitic in particular.

(Alberta Hansard,
May 12, 1983, p.921)

[
25
]

These views, and comments to the like effect,
were widely reported. The Alberta members of Parliament also published a public disavowal.

[
26
]

We do not criticize the then Premier. This is
not

a case like
R. v. Vermette
(1988)
1988 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, 41 C.C.C. (3d) 523 (S.C.C.). No
criminal charges had then been laid, and he relied on a decision of a civil
court. He simply spoke out in an obvious and legitimate effort to dissociate
the government and people of Alberta from what the civil court had found that this accused had done.

[
27
]

But, if the Premier had been concerned in 1983,
so also it seems to us must have been the neighbours of the accused in the
judicial district of Red Deer when the trial opened in 1985. Yet from them this
jury was to be selected. That kind of concern puts understandable pressure on a
juror, and it is a pressure that
might
cause one to fail the oath. In
our view, if challenge for cause is ever to be permitted, it must be in a case
like this. It was not frivolous in this circumstance to test a prospective
juror on the question whether he or she might feel constrained to convict the
accused in order to demonstrate the innocence of the
community
in the
eyes of the world.

[
28
]

It is said for the Crown that the appellant
should not be able to challenge jurors on the basis of pre-trial publicity when
he refused to avail himself of a publication ban at the preliminary hearing.
This may well be the case if that were the only publicity. But, as we have
demonstrated, this is not the case. The publicity to which we refer existed for
two years before the preliminary hearing.

[
29
]

We do not wish to be taken as going so far as
suggesting that it was or is impossible for the accused to get a fair trial by
reason of this publicity. But that is quite different from rejecting, as this
trial judge did, the possibility that one prospective juror
might
not be
indifferent. That was in the circumstances of this case a legitimate subject of
inquiry.

[
30
]

The accused made a Charter attack on similar lines.
But the Charter offers no new protection from an unfair trial in cases like
this, it merely guarantees the present rules. We need say no more.

[
31
]

In the result, the conviction must be quashed
and a new trial must be ordered.

II.

[
32
]

In another ground, the accused said that the
learned trial judge mis-directed the jury about the mental element required for
this crime. The argument was that the bolded sections of this passage contained
error:

By using the word wilfully in this
section Parliament is emphasizing that the accused must be found to have
intended each specific ingredient of the offence before he can be found guilty.
There can be no argument about the nature of the intention that must be proven.
It must be shown that the accused in "communicating statements" knew
and intended to engage in promotion, that he knew and intended that what he was
promoting was hatred and that he knew and intended that the hatred be directed
against the Jewish people. If you have a reasonable doubt as to his knowledge
and intention as to any one of the elements, he is entitled to a verdict of not
guilty.

You can see that an acquittal does not
necessarily mean there was no promotion of hatred against the Jewish people.
That alone is not enough for a conviction. You must be further convinced that,
if there was such promotion, the accused acted wilfully throughout.

Whether or not the existence of
wilfulness is proven beyond reasonable doubt will of course be determined by
you after weighing the evidence. As I stated earlier a fact can be proven by
drawing inferences. In this area of wilfulness and intention, you might infer
that because the Defendant made certain statements and from the surrounding
circumstances, he must have intended to promote hatred against the Jewish
people. That of course is for you to decide. If the evidence is such that you
have a reasonable doubt as to the making of the statements or of the
surrounding circumstances then of course you could not draw the inference. Even
if you are convinced as to the existence of the surrounding circumstances and
the giving of the statements or the making of the statements you must still be
convinced that the inference is the correct one before you can rely on it.

The important thing to remember is that
intention must be proven. A crime cannot be committed accidentally.
Of
course, if you were to find that the Defendant in his actions was aware that
there was a danger that his conduct would bring about the promotion of hatred
against the Jewish people and that knowing that, he chose to persist in it
despite the risk, you would then make a finding of wilfulness. If a person
knowingly seeks the risk of criminal activity and takes a chance he cannot be
said to be acting without intention
.

Or if you are to find that the accused
deliberately kept himself ignorant of the results of his activities after
realizing what those results might be, then provided he has intentionally so
blinded himself to reality, the law presumes he has full knowledge, and he
would be found to be acting wilfully.

Be careful, though. In either case it is
not enough to say the accused was careless or negligent about discovering what
he was doing or reasonable people would have known what the results of the
teachings would be. That is not enough. It is the personal knowledge of the
accused that is important. Wilfulness must be found beyond reasonable doubt to
have existed one way or another in the mind of the accused before you can bring
in a verdict of guilty.

Before leaving the question of wilfulness
I think I should say a word about the issues of truth and motivation. The
sincerity and honesty of the accused is of course to be considered by you in
determining the credibility of his evidence.
But it is not a defence to the
wilfulness aspect of this charge for an accused person to say that he thought
he was speaking the truth or that he was otherwise highly motivated. If it is
found that he indeed knowingly promoted hatred against the Jewish people, if he
knew he was doing that, the wilfulness of the act is not changed because he may
have thought the statements were true or that he was highly motivated. If you
are convinced that the Defendant knew he was making those statements, that he
knew those statements promoted hatred and that he knew the hatred was directed
against the Jewish people, then even if he did so as a result of what he
honestly believed were the highest purposes, he must be found to have acted
wilfully.
You would then have to convict him unless his case falls within
one of the statutory defences I'll now discuss with you.

[
33
]

The defence here contended that the learned
trial judge did not adequately warn the jury that, for guilt, they must be
satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that this accused knew as a fact that his
words would cause hatred.

[
34
]

In the passage cited, the learned trial judge
first suggested that the charging section required both actual knowledge that
hatred would result
and
the desire that people hate. The question arises
whether both or either are sufficient for guilt. Three possibilities exist:
First, an accused might strongly desire to promote hatred
and
know for a
fact that what he says will accomplish his desires. Second, an accused might
strongly desire to stir hatred, but be unsure whether his efforts will be
effective. The third possibility is the converse of the second: an accused
might know perfectly well that his words will cause hatred, but not desire that
result. Usually a defence of this last sort will raise a question about means
and ends. The accused will say that any causation of hatred was ancillary to
his real intent. Sometimes this is put forward as a "higher motive"
defence. This was the situation in
Buzzanga and Durocher
(1979)
1979 CanLII 1927 (ON CA)
, 49
C.C.C. (2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.).
The curious facts of that case were that the immature accused, who wished to
stir support for pro-French causes, disseminated crude and cruel anti-French
literature door-to-door in the desire to unleash a backlash.

[
35
]

Martin, J.A. in
Buzzanga
considered all
three of the possibilities we mention. He accepted that the weight of authority
affirmed that the mental element for wilfulness was always met if it could be
shown that an accused desired the forbidden result whether or not he knew it
was going to occur. The more difficult question was whether guilt existed when
the accused did not desire the result but in fact foresaw it. After a review of
the authorities, he concluded at page 384-5:

I agree, however (assuming without
deciding that there may be cases in which intended consequences are confined to
those which it is the actor's conscious purpose to bring about), that, as a
general rule, a person who foresees that a consequence is certain or
substantially certain to result from an act which he does in order to achieve
some other purpose, intends that consequence. The actor's foresight of the
certainty or moral certainty of the consequence resulting from his conduct
compels a conclusion that if he, none the less, acted so as to produce it, then
he decided to bring it about (albeit regretfully), in order to achieve his ultimate
purpose. His intention encompasses the means as well as to his ultimate
objective.

[
36
]

In the decision of the Supreme Court from the
original Reasons of this Court, that view is affirmed. Dickson, C.J.C. (as he
then was) said, speaking for the majority:

In "promotes" we thus have a
word that indicates more than simple encouragement or advancement. The
hatemonger must
intend or foresee as substantially certain
a direct and
active stimulation of hatred against an identifiable group.

[emphasis
added]

[
37
]

We therefore conclude that the learned trial
judge, in the opening of the passage, over-stated the test. An accused need not
both intend, in the sense of desire, and foresee as a certainty. It is enough
that he did
either.
But that overcharge, of itself, cannot help the
accused. Nor is it comfort to the accused on appeal that he never put the
alternate intent (no desire but foresight to a certainty) to the jury.

[
38
]

The problem raised by the accused arose later,
when the learned trial judge told the jury that they could infer an intention,
in the sense of desire, from an awareness of a
mere chance
that people
will hate. He said, and we repeat it for convenience:

Of course, if you were to find that the
Defendant in his actions was aware that there was a danger that his conduct
would cause the promotion of hatred against the Jewish people and that knowing
that, he chose to persist in it despite the risk, you would then make a finding
of wilfulness. If a person knowingly seeks the risk of criminal activity and
takes a chance he cannot be said to be acting without intention.

[
39
]

We accept that a charge about "risk"
and "danger" is very different from one about "substantial
certainty". If this passage was indeed a charge about the alternate intent
it would be inadequate. But it is not. It is about the undeniable ability of
the jury to infer intent in the sense of desire from the circumstances present
in the case, which might include awareness of a risk, but not a certainty, what
the result will be.

[
40
]

Nevertheless it contains a dangerous error. The
best that can be said to a jury is that they should
consider
the risk
known to the accused on the question whether they should infer desire from the
circumstances. To say that "a person who takes a risk cannot be said to
act without intention" is to take the issue away from the jury. It is for
the jury to decide, in this case, whether that is the correct conclusion. The
learned trial judge, in that sentence, treated a question of fact as though it
were a question of law. It may be said that this was innocuous error. Most of
the time we accept that people desire consequences that they know they will
cause. As the curious facts in
Buzzanga

demonstrate, this is not always
the case.

[
41
]

We accept that the impugned statement was both
prefaced and followed by statements that more correctly instructed the jury.
They did not quite erase the blunt suggestion that the jury
must
infer
the required intent if there was awareness of any risk that what the accused
said might cause hatred.

[
42
]

This error was critical here. The accused had
admitted that he had made remarks to his students that were highly critical.
The evidence of some students was that they came to hate Jews because of them.
The accused, however, protested in his defence that he had proclaimed the truth
as he saw it. We think a jury would quickly conclude on this evidence that the
accused must have been aware at least of the
risk
he was causing hatred.
Had they pursued in their deliberations, they might well have concluded he knew
this to a certainty. They might well also have concluded that he must have
intended that result. But this charge told them they were not required to enter
those deliberations. They were told that it was enough to conclude that he knew
the risk was there, whatever his desire and whatever his level of knowledge
beyond that. We do not know whether they limited their deliberations, but it is
possible that they did.

[
43
]

In the ordinary course, we would now proceed to
consider whether to invoke s. 686(1)(b)(iii) C.C.C. This would involve our
deciding whether this jury, properly instructed, would in any event have
convicted. We think it inappropriate for us to offer our own assessment of the
evidence in a case where, for other reasons, we think a new trial must be
ordered. Therefore, we shall say nothing about this issue.

III

[
44
]

Beyond the free speech issue and the presumption
of innocence issue and the two grounds just dealt with, the accused presented
many other grounds of appeal. Some were in the factum, some were made for the
first time in oral argument. Many overlapped. The first factum offered 30
grounds plus eight "supplementary" grounds. Asked to re-file, counsel
put them into
groups
of grounds - but then added more grounds. As we
have already said, none had merit. To temper the length of these Reasons, we
shall only deal with those that might have led to an acquittal if accepted.
Those whose remedy would be a new trial can we think be left alone as no longer
material in the light of the first part of these Reasons.

[
45
]

Two groups had to do with evidential issues, one
with allegations against the prosecution, one with charge errors, and two with
procedural errors. Of the evidential matters, one group complained of improper
exclusion. Even if correct, and they were not, these matters would only lead to
a new trial. This also can be said of charge errors. The ground alleging
inconsistent verdicts, which might in some circumstances lead to an acquittal,
is, on examination, in reality about an alleged charging error.

[
46
]

Another ground invokes s.11(g) of the Charter,
which protects an accused from condemnation under
ex post facto
laws.
The provision in the
Code
under review was, of course, in force during
the charge period. His argument is that it had not, in all respects, been
interpreted by the courts, and therefore the accused did not know the law
against him. This is akin to a void-for-vagueness argument. See
Jahelka

(1987)
1987 ABCA 153 (CanLII)
, 54 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 at 12 (C.A.). It is not clear at all that such a rule exists in Canada under the aegis of s. 7. If it does,
it should resemble the "prescribed by law" test for s. 1. That test,
in turn, demands that the legislation be "intelligible". See
Irwin
Toy
(1989)
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, 94 N.R. 167 (S.C.C.) at 229. That test is met here. The dispute
among courts about the constitutional validity of this law should not be
misunderstood. No great dispute existed about its meaning. The provisions in
question are capable of interpretation. This ground fails.

[
47
]

One ground complained that the learned trial
judge took judicial notice that "Judaism is a religion, and that Judaism
is the religion of the Jewish people in general." We appreciate that this
statement does not make distinctions that the accused would make. It is not
error to assert a notorious fact just because an accused denies it. In any
event, even if taking judicial notice was an error, the only result could be a
new trial. The Crown clearly intended to lead evidence if the judge did not
take notice, and would be entitled to a new trial if he erred.

[
48
]

It is said in a related ground that the verdict
was inconsistent with the notice taken. The best we can make of this is that,
because the "target" group was defined by religion, the defence of
"religious belief" automatically was engaged. This is patent
nonsense. Attacks on religious groups need not by definition, and often are not
in fact, based upon contradictory religious beliefs as opposed to, say, false
statements of historical fact.

[
49
]

Another ground attacked the validity of a
pre-trial seizure of papers of the accused, and delay in their return. But the
accused did not bring this complaint home to the trial. He did not demonstrate
convincingly that his ability to defend had been impaired in a significant way,
or that the trial itself was in any way unfair on that account. As a result,
the seizure matter is irrelevant.

[
50
]

One group of evidential grounds raised questions
about improper exclusion of evidence. The items complained of were peripheral
to the Crown case. To gain an acquittal on such a ground, the accused must not
only show improper exclusion but also that the balance of the evidence could
not sustain a conviction. Significantly, no ground suggested in terms that the
verdict was unreasonable.

[
51
]

One group of attacks was about prosecutorial
behaviour. To obtain an acquittal on such a ground the accused must show a
great deal more than error or occasional lapses. In any event, we see no merit
in any of these grounds. Most of them were in fact about rulings of the trial
judge, not about the behaviour of counsel. Counsel did suggest Crown improper briefing.
The learned trial judge held a
voir dire
on the issue, and decided that
the Crown had not been shown to be guilty of any impropriety. We find his
conclusions persuasive on the evidence before him.

[
52
]

A supplementary ground suggested inflammatory
remarks and error during the Crown address. Whether this was so, we see nothing
that would offer a ground of acquittal.

[
53
]

One ground contended that it was not right that
the accused be cross-examined by reference to text-books not already in
evidence. The use of that sort of cross-examination is very limited, and error
may have been committed here. That would in no way lead to an argument about
acquittal.

[
54
]

One ground claimed unreasonable delay, and a
quashing order was sought. The delay complained of
then
was not after
charge but before charge. The Supreme Court has limited the Charter remedy to
after-charge delay. See
Carter
(1986)
1986 CanLII 18 (SCC)
, 26 C.C.C. (3d) 572 and
Mills

(1986)
1986 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, 26 C.C.C.(3d) 481.

[
55
]

Another was inadequate particulars. The
information was adequate, and any other details to which the accused was
entitled were disclosed to him during the preliminary hearing.

[
56
]

Another ground was the impossibility of a fair
trial after the condemnation of the accused by the civil court and high
governmental officials. On a pre-trial motion, a quashing of the information
for pre-trial publicity was denied by Quigley, J. See
R. v. Keegstra

1984 19 C.C.C. (3d) p. 254. We agree with that disposition, and reject the
suggestion that the accused could not receive a fair trial. See
Vermette
.

IV.

[
57
]

The publication of Supplementary Reasons for
Judgment more than two years after the publication of the original is unusual
and requires an explanation.

[
58
]

The unanimous original Reasons, published on June 6, 1988, decided that the charging section
must be declared of no legal effect because it was in contradiction of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. See
R. v. Keegstra
(1988)
1988 ABCA 234 (CanLII)
, 43
C.C.C. (3d) 150. Having come to that conclusion, the appropriate disposition
was that the indictment be quashed. We then added, at 179-180:

In the result, we need not deal with the
several dozen other grounds of appeal raised by Mr. Christie in his several
factums. It should be noted that none had the slightest merit except those
relating to the failure of the learned trial judge to charge that recklessness
whether hatred might result was not sufficient for conviction, in compliance
with the rule in
Buzzanga
, and his failure to permit a challenge for
cause because of the inordinate pretrial publicity, a previously unclear point
settled since the trial by
Zundel.

[
59
]

Leave to appeal from that decision was granted
by the Supreme Court of Canada, and that Court, in Reasons for Decision
published December 20, 1990, reversed the Charter decision of this Court. As a
consequence, the other issues suddenly became necessary for decision. The
Supreme Court of Canada decided to refer them to this Court rather than decide
them itself. Chief Justice Dickson (as he then was), speaking for the majority,
said at p. 105-106 of the unreported decision:

I would thus reverse the decision of the
Alberta Court of Appeal and allow the appeal. This case should return to the
Court of Appeal in order to resolve those issues left unexamined by reason of
its decision to strike down the impugned provisions.

[
60
]

We do not understand that the Supreme Court, in
this order, has referred this matter to us for further argument or
deliberation. The issues in question were fully canvassed before the Court when
the matter first came before us. Moreover, the panel had made a decision about
these issues. It was only the publication of reasons that were withheld and
that because the Court mistakenly thought those issues had become moot.

[
61
]

It seems, therefore, appropriate for the Court
now to publish the decision then concurred in. The reasons above are
essentially a re-statement of the reasons agreed upon by the panel at that
time.

62
]

Court nevertheless are competent to decide the question by virtue of the
Court
of Appeal Act
, R.S.A. 1980, c. C-28 s. 8(a).
